n: The book opens by naming its source: this message came from the Lord to a prophet named Joel. We know almost nothing else about him, and scholars disagree about exactly when he lived.

f.g: His name means “Jehovah is God.”

n: Joel calls on the oldest people in the land to remember: has anything like this disaster ever happened before? The answer is no — this is unheard of.

f.g: Or “elders” — the senior leaders whose memories reached furthest back.

n: This catastrophe is so great it must be told to children and grandchildren for generations. Joel wants its lesson about turning to God passed down.
Wave after wave of locusts has stripped the land. Whatever one swarm left, the next devoured, until nothing remained. The four names may describe different kinds or growth stages of locusts.

f.g: The four Hebrew words (gazam, arbeh, yeleq, ḥasil) are all names for locusts, perhaps at different stages of life.

n: Those who live for drink are told to wake up and weep, because the vines are gone and there will be no new wine. Joel uses the disaster to shake people out of careless living.

f.g: Fresh grape juice just pressed from the harvest.

n: The locusts are pictured as an invading nation — countless and powerful, with teeth like a lion’s. Something small becomes terrifying when it comes in overwhelming numbers.

f.g: The Lord speaks of Israel as His own land.
Molars or jaw teeth — grinding teeth that chew everything.

n: The locusts have stripped the vines and gnawed the bark off the fig trees, leaving the branches bare and white. The vine and fig tree were symbols of Israel’s peace and prosperity.

f.g: Stripped the bark from.

n: The land should mourn like a young bride whose husband has died. Sackcloth was rough goat-hair cloth worn as a sign of grief.

f.g: Here a young woman betrothed or newly married; her loss is especially bitter.
Coarse, dark cloth worn in mourning or repentance.

n: With crops gone, there is nothing to offer at the temple. Even the daily worship is interrupted, and the priests grieve because they cannot perform their service.

f.g: “Meat” in KJV means food; this is the grain (flour) offering.

n: The three staple crops of the land — grain, wine, and olive oil — have all failed. Even the land itself seems to mourn.

f.g: KJV “corn” means grain, such as wheat or barley — not American maize.
Withers; grows weak.

n: Farmers and vineyard workers are told to wail because the whole harvest is lost. Their hard work has come to nothing.

f.g: Farmers; those who till the ground.

n: Every fruit tree has withered — and with them people’s joy. Joel links the outward drought to an inward emptiness among the people.

f.g: The Hebrew tappuaḥ may mean apple, apricot, or quince.

n: Joel turns to the priests and urges them to put on sackcloth and spend the night in mourning prayer. Spiritual leaders should lead the way in repentance.

f.g: Put on (sackcloth) — tie it around the waist.

n: Here is the remedy: call a holy fast, gather everyone to the temple, and cry to the Lord. When disaster strikes, God’s people turn to Him together.

f.g: A sacred gathering of the whole community for worship and prayer.

n: The locust plague is a warning sign of something bigger: “the day of the Lord,” a time when God steps in to judge. This phrase is a major theme of Joel’s book.

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai; there is a wordplay: “destruction” (shod) from “the Almighty” (Shaddai).

n: Joel points to what everyone can see: the food is gone, and the joyful feasts at the temple have stopped.

f.g: Food.

n: Seeds have shriveled in the dry ground, and storehouses stand empty and broken because there is nothing to put in them.

f.g: Granaries; storehouses for grain.
Lumps of dry earth.

n: Even the animals suffer. Herds wander confused, and flocks starve without pasture. The whole creation feels the effects of the disaster.

f.g: Wandering in confusion.

n: Joel himself prays, setting an example. Drought and heat have scorched the land as if it had been burned by fire.

f.w: O LORD, to thee will I cry

n: Even the wild animals seem to look to God, panting for water because the streams have dried up. If animals cry to God, how much more should His people?
